catalog_quote: Thus Zaysete is a tonal language because the use of different pitch brings meaning change. ... Hayward (1990) mentioned tone in his studies simply by brief statements with some examples. He said that Zaysete (East Ometo) is a tonal-accent language in which tone and accent interact at the phrasal level. Isolated words have the following possible pitch contours: LL, HH, LH, HL and LHL. On the other hand, Mulugeta (1988: 30) tried to explain stress, pitch and intonation in Zaysete. According to Mulugeta, the stress pattern is associated with the pitch pattern i.e. the stronger the stress the higher the pitch, and the lower the stress, the weaker the pitch. Moreover, two pitch levels are identified - high and low. Though, Mulugeta has never mentioned about tone. ... my data also reveals Zaysete has two basic tones, high (H) and low (L). ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Zaysete is described as a two-tone (H, L) language whose lexical nouns and adjectives carry exactly one high tone, lexically placed on either the final or the penultimate vowel (unpredictable); disyllabic verbs have the H on the first or last syllable and polysyllabic verbs/adjectives on the second/penultimate; pronouns may have more than one H. The only stress statement is second-hand: Mulugeta 1988:30 (per Bogale) says stress goes with high pitch. Hayward 1990 (per Bogale) and Azeb Amha 2014 (first-hand, p. 170, mainly Zargulla data) treat the language as tonal-accent (pitch accent) because of the culminative, restricted distribution of H in polysyllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Pronouns have more than one H per word (p. 57); verb tonal patterns depend on verb class (o-class vs a-class; Hayward 1990:300, Bogale p. 55); pitch and accent interact at the phrase level per Hayward 1990 (as reported).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, isolated simple (unsuffixed) words elicited in citation form; Bogale notes that tone-accent interaction is phrasal per Hayward but does not analyse it. The stress remark is Bogale's report of Mulugeta 1988:30, not her own analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Bogale 2017 describes Zaysete (Zayse proper, spoken west of Lake Chamo near Arba Minch; c. 21,000 speakers). Azeb Amha 2014 treats Zayse and Zargulla as two dialects of one language and draws most examples from Zargulla, taking Zayse data from Hayward 1990/1999; both fall under glottocode zays1235 (no separate Glottolog dialect codes listed).

sources.note: p. 170: 'Contrast in tone is attested in some words (e.g., keesé "a house" vs. kéewe "to bid prices"); however, Zg.-Zs. are analysed as tone-accent languages because of the predictable distribution and restrictions on high tone in multisyllabic words.' Vowel length and gemination contrastive. Mostly Zargulla data; Zayse data from Hayward 1990, 1999. No stress statement.
